name: Crew cut

lead: The crew cut is a short men's haircut in which the hair on top is cut relatively short and graduated from longest at the front hairline to shortest at the crown, with the sides and back tapered short. It reads as neat, athletic and low-maintenance.
People use it as a clean frame for the face with minimal styling. It has a long history, from college rowing teams to the US military, and has no research behind it as a look.

paras: A barber cuts it with clippers and guards or scissors, with the sides and back tapered and the top kept longer, usually under about an inch to an inch and a half in classic versions. Common variants are the flat top, the longer Ivy League cut, and the butch. Maintenance is regular trims to keep the taper clean.
There are no health risks specific to the cut. Very short hair shows scalp features such as scars or birthmarks and offers less sun protection for the scalp.

angle.text: The crew cut gives a clean, structured outline that needs little styling. The short length means little daily styling.

lead: The crew cut is a men's haircut in which the upright hair on top is cut relatively short, graduated from longest at the front hairline to shortest at the back of the crown, with the sides and back tapered [1]. Variants include the shorter butch, the longer Ivy League cut and the flat top [1].
The style is used for a tidy, low-maintenance look, and is tied in popular imagery to short, practical styling [1]. Crew cuts, flat tops, butches and Ivy League cuts are all classed as buzz cuts [1].
It is associated with college rowing, the military, and mid-century American style. No study has tested its effect on perceived attractiveness.
infobox: Short and graduated, longest at front hairline [1]
US college crew teams and military (early twentieth century)

paras: The classic crew cut has a top that approaches a horizontal profile, with sides and back tapered to short, semi-short or medium lengths [1]. Grokipedia describes typical sides of about 1/8 to 1/4 inch with a top of roughly half an inch to an inch and a half, and says it differs from the buzz cut by keeping slightly longer hair on top [2].
The short crew cut is sometimes called a butch, though a butch usually has uniform top length. The Ivy League cut is a longer-topped version, and the flat top forms a level plane [1].

The style was known earlier as the short pompadour and the brush cut. The name 'crew haircut' was probably coined for the short hair worn by rowers at universities such as Harvard, Yale, Princeton and Cornell, whose short hair stayed out of the face [1]. Grokipedia attributes the popularising of the cut to Yale oarsman John Hay Whitney in the late 1920s [2].

Crew cuts were popular among US college students in the 1920s and 1930s, and men drafted in World War II received G.I. haircuts, with many keeping crew cuts afterward [1]. The style waned as long hair became popular from the mid-1960s, returned in the late 1970s and early 1980s, and the flat top was the most popular variant in the 1980s [1].
The crew cut is linked to military styling and to a collegiate image from rowing and the Ivy League. Author Jack Kerouac is pictured with a G.I. crew cut in 1943 [1].
No studies found. PubMed results for 'crew cut' concern an unrelated polymer-chemistry term.

timeline.event: Yale's championship football team appears with close-cropped heads, as long football hair goes out of style [1].
Crew cuts become popular among US college students, especially in the Ivy League [1].
G.I. haircuts in World War II lead many men to keep crew cuts [1].
The style returns; flat top is the most popular variant in the 1980s [1].
